items.title: Figure 3 prompt, A comet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Its distance from the Sun is 0.60 AU at perihelion and 4.2 AU at aphelion. Explain why the equal-time areas have different shapes, and find the ratio of its speeds at these two points.

body.html: 𝑟<sub>p</sub> = 0.60 AU, 𝑟<sub>a</sub> = 4.2 AU. Unknown: the shape difference and 𝑣<sub>p</sub> / 𝑣<sub>a</sub>.

Kepler's second law: the line from the Sun to the comet sweeps equal areas in equal times. At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so a thin wedge has area ≈<sup>1</sup> <sub>2</sub>𝑟(𝑣𝛥𝑡).
Set the two equal-time wedge areas equal:
Near the Sun the radius is short, so the arc must be long (fast, short and wide wedge). Far away the radius is long, so the arc is short (slow, long and narrow wedge).

answer.html: The wedges have equal area but different shapes: short and wide at perihelion, long and narrow at aphelion. The comet moves 7.0 times faster at perihelion than at aphelion.

check.html: The comet is 7 times closer at perihelion and 7 times faster, so 𝑟𝑣 is the same at both points, as equal areas require.

items.title: Get It? (Kepler's first law), A newly discovered moon orbits Saturn. What does Kepler's first law say about the shape of its path and where Saturn is located?

answer.html: The moon's path is an ellipse, and Saturn (the central body) sits at one focus of that ellipse, not necessarily at its center.

items.title: Get It? (gravity explains orbits), Summarize how gravitational force explains a moon orbiting Jupiter.

answer.html: Jupiter's gravity pulls the moon toward Jupiter. Because the moon is also moving sideways, the pull does not bring it down; it continuously changes the moon's direction so it follows a closed path. Setting gravity equal to the centripetal force, G𝑚<sub>J</sub>𝑚/ 𝑟<sup>2</sup> = 𝑚(4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>), gives 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = (4𝜋<sup>2</sup> / G𝑚<sub>J</sub>)𝑟<sup>3</sup>, which is Kepler's third law for Jupiter's moons.

items.title: D at 𝑟= 1.90 AU with 𝑇= 1038 d. Do these planets obey Kepler's third law?

body.html: Kepler's third law says 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> is the same constant for every body orbiting one central object.

Compute 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> in AU<sup>3</sup> / day<sup>2</sup>: Planet 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> B 6.37 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> C 6.37 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> D 6.37 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> The three values agree to better than 0.2%.

answer.html: Yes. 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> is essentially the same for all three planets, so they obey Kepler's third law.

check.html: Three planets spanning a factor of 38 in distance giving the same constant is strong evidence.

For Earth: 𝑟= 1.00 AU, 𝑇= 365.25 d, so 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = 7.50 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> AU<sup>3</sup> / day<sup>2</sup> (this is the Sun, 1 𝑀<sub>Sun</sub>).

items.title: CCC: Patterns (Lesson 3 tag; Cavendish), Create a presentation explaining how the patterns in Galileo's observations of Jupiter's moons provide evidence that the same gravity law applies to Earth's Moon and to satellites.

body.html: The pattern 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = constant seen for Jupiter's moons is the same pattern that Newton's law predicts for anything orbiting a single central body. Work (outline for a presentation): 1. Observation: Io (𝑇= 1.77 d, 𝑟= 4.22 × 10<sup>5</sup> km) and Callisto (𝑇= 16.7 d, 𝑟= 1.88 × 10<sup>6</sup> km) give 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = 2.40 × 10<sup>16</sup> and 2.38 × 10<sup>16</sup> km<sup>3</sup> / d<sup>2</sup>, the same within 1%. 2. Explanation: gravity supplies the centripetal force, so 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = G𝑚<sub>J</sub> / 4𝜋<sup>2</sup> depends only on the central mass. 3. Same pattern, other places: Earth's Moon and artificial satellites also obey 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = constant, with a different constant because Earth has a different mass. 4. Conclusion: one law of gravity, with the mass of the central body setting the constant, governs moons, satellites and planets.

answer.html: (Outline above.) Key claim: the same 𝑟<sup>3</sup> / 𝑇<sup>2</sup> pattern appears around every central body, which shows that one gravitational law operates at every scale.

items.title: Check Your Progress 11, The Cavendish experiment is repeated with two aluminum spheres in a lab at the top of a mountain. Would the value of G that is measured be the same or different?

body.html: G = 𝐹𝑟<sup>2</sup> / (𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub>) is a universal constant. The force depends only on the masses and the distance between centers, not on the material or on where the lab is.

When the force is measured for known masses and spacing, the combination 𝐹𝑟<sup>2</sup> / (𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub>) always comes out the same. Aluminum spheres are less dense than lead, so they take up more room, but only the center-to-center distance matters. The mountain changes the local 𝑔 slightly, but G does not depend on 𝑔.

answer.html: The same. G is a universal constant independent of the material and location; only the masses and the center-to-center distance matter.

items.title: Check Your Progress 12, Laws or theories? General relativity is called a theory. Was it ever a law, and will it ever become a law?

body.html: In science, a law summarizes a pattern, usually as an equation, and tells what happens. A theory is a well-tested explanation of why it happens. A theory does not "graduate" into a law; they are different kinds of statements.

General relativity explains why masses attract (mass curves space) and makes predictions such as light bending. It is an explanation, not a one-line rule for the size of the force. A law like Newton's 𝐹= G𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub> / 𝑟<sup>2</sup> is a rule describing what happens, and it emerges from general relativity for weak fields.

answer.html: No. It was never a law and will not become one. A law describes what happens; a theory explains why, and the two do not turn into each other.

items.title: Figure 3 prompt, "Explain why the equal time areas are shaped differently."

body.html: Kepler's second law: the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. The planet moves faster when close to the Sun and slower when far away.

A thin triangle-like wedge has area ≈<sup>1</sup> <sup>2</sup>(radius)(arc length). Near the Sun the radius is short, so to get the same area the arc must be long: the planet travels a long arc in the time interval (fast), giving a short, wide wedge. Far from the Sun the radius is long, so the arc must be short (slow), giving a long, narrow wedge.

answer.html: The areas have the same size but different shapes: close to the Sun they are short and wide (long arc, short radius, high speed); far from the Sun they are long and narrow (short arc, long radius, low speed).

check.html: Equal area with a larger radius requires a shorter arc, which matches "slower when farther."

items.title: Get It? (Kepler's first law), Describe the common feature that Kepler's first law found concerning the paths of orbiting objects.

items.title: Get It? (gravity explains orbits), Summarize how gravitational force explains a planet orbiting the Sun.

answer.html: The Sun's gravity pulls the planet toward the Sun. Because the planet is also moving sideways, this pull does not bring it into the Sun; it continuously changes the planet's direction so it moves in a closed path. Setting gravity equal to the centripetal force, G𝑚<sub>S</sub>𝑚<sub>p</sub> / 𝑟<sup>2</sup> = 𝑚<sub>p</sub>(4𝜋<sup>2</sup>𝑟/ 𝑇<sup>2</sup>), gives 𝑇<sup>2</sup> = (4𝜋<sup>2</sup> / G𝑚<sub>S</sub>)𝑟<sup>3</sup>, which is Kepler's third law.

answer.html: 𝑀≈1.32 times the Sun's mass

items.title: CCC: Patterns (Lesson 3 tag; Cavendish), Create a presentation explaining how the patterns Cavendish observed in a small-scale experiment provide evidence for solar- system-scale interactions.

body.html: The same law, 𝐹= G𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub> / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>, was seen in the lab and applies in space. Work (outline for a presentation): 1. Cavendish measured the tiny attraction between lead spheres and found it grew with the masses and shrank with the square of the separation; this gave G = 6.67 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> N·m<sup>2</sup> / kg<sup>2</sup>. 2. Same pattern, large scale: with that G, 𝑔= G𝑚<sub>E</sub> / 𝑟<sub>E</sub> <sup>2</sup> gives Earth's mass, 𝑚<sub>E</sub> = 𝑔𝑟<sub>E</sub> <sup>2</sup> / G = 5.98 × 10<sup>24</sup> kg (book value). 3. The pattern predicts planetary motion: 𝑇= 2𝜋√𝑟<sup>3</sup> / G𝑚<sup>S</sup> reproduces Kepler's third law (Neptune: 165 yr). 4. Conclusion: one pattern holds from lead balls in a lab to planets, so the same law governs the solar system.

answer.html: (Outline above.) Key claim: the lab-scale proportionality 𝐹∝𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub> / 𝑟<sup>2</sup> and the measured G reproduce the observed planetary motions, which shows the same law operates at every scale.

items.title: Check Your Progress 8, Neptune's orbital period

body.html: 𝑟= 4.496 × 10<sup>12</sup> m (Figure 9), 𝑚<sub>S</sub> = 1.99 × 10<sup>30</sup> kg, G = 6.67 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>11</sup> N·m<sup>2</sup> / kg<sup>2</sup>. Unknown 𝑇.
Gravity supplies the centripetal force, which gives 𝑇= 2𝜋√𝑟<sup>3</sup> / (G𝑚<sup>S</sup>).
Convert to years: 5.20 × 10<sup>9</sup> s ÷ (3.156 × 10<sup>7</sup> s/yr) = 165 yr.

answer.html: 𝑇≈5.20 × 10<sup>9</sup> s ≈165 years

check.html: Kepler's third law with Earth: 30.05<sup>1.5</sup> = 164.7 years. Agrees.

items.title: Check Your Progress 9, Force between two 15-kg balls, 35 cm apart; fraction of one ball's weight

body.html: 𝑚<sub>1</sub> = 𝑚<sub>2</sub> = 15 kg, 𝑟= 0.35 m. Unknown 𝐹<sub>g</sub> and 𝐹<sub>g</sub> / 𝑊.
Law of universal gravitation, 𝐹<sub>g</sub> = G𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub> / 𝑟<sup>2</sup>; weight 𝑊= 𝑚𝑔.

answer.html: 𝐹<sub>g</sub> ≈1.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> N, which is about 8.3 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>10</sup> (under a billionth) of one ball's weight.

check.html: Matches the book's bowling-ball example (3.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>8</sup> N for 7.26 kg at 0.30 m): smaller masses give a smaller force.

items.title: Check Your Progress 10, If Earth shrank but kept its mass, what happens to 𝑔 at the surface?

body.html: 𝑔= G𝑚<sub>E</sub> / 𝑟<sub>E</sub> <sup>2</sup> .
𝑚<sub>E</sub> is unchanged and 𝑟<sub>E</sub> decreases. Since 𝑔∝1 / 𝑟<sub>E</sub> <sup>2</sup> , a smaller radius makes 𝑔 larger. For example, halving the radius would quadruple 𝑔.

answer.html: 𝑔 would increase (in proportion to 1 / 𝑟<sub>E</sub> <sup>2</sup> ).

check.html: Being closer to the center of the same mass means a stronger pull.

items.title: Check Your Progress 11, Would G be the same or different with copper spheres of equal mass?

body.html: G = 𝐹𝑟<sup>2</sup> / (𝑚<sub>1</sub>𝑚<sub>2</sub>) is a universal constant. The force depends only on the masses and the distance between centers, not on what the material is.

Equal masses at the same spacing give the same force, hence the same G. (Copper is less dense than lead, so the spheres would be larger, but if center spacing and masses are the same the force is the same.)

answer.html: The same. G is a universal constant independent of the material; only the masses and the center-to-center distance matter.

items.title: Check Your Progress 12, Laws or theories? Were Kepler's statements and Newton's equation ever theories? Will they ever become theories?

body.html: In science, a law summarizes a pattern, usually as an equation, and tells what happens. A theory is a well-tested explanation of why it happens. A law does not "graduate" into a theory; they are different kinds of statements.

Kepler's laws describe Tycho's data (how planets move, not why). Newton's law gives the size of the force but does not explain how it acts at a distance. Both are explained by a theory: Newton's law is the weak-field limit of Einstein's general theory of relativity.

answer.html: No. They were descriptions of what happens, not explanations of why, so they were never theories and will not become theories. Einstein's general relativity is the theory that explains them.

items.title: Check Your Progress 13 (Critical Thinking), Rock thrown horizontally on the Moon

body.html: The rock is a projectile with a horizontal speed 𝑣 and a downward acceleration equal to the local 𝑔. The Moon's 𝑔 is about 1.6 N/kg, much less than Earth's 9.8 N/kg.

Fall time from height ℎ is 𝑡= √2ℎ/ 𝑔, and range is 𝑥= 𝑣𝑡. With a smaller 𝑔, 𝑡 is longer, so the rock travels farther horizontally. For the same 𝑣 and ℎ, 𝑥<sup>Moon</sup> / 𝑥<sup>Earth</sup> = √9.80 / 1.62 = 2.5. The path is still a parabola, but flatter and wider.

answer.html: The Moon's weaker gravity bends the path downward more slowly, so the rock stays in the air longer and lands about 2.5 times farther away than on Earth (same throw, same height). The path is a flatter parabola.

check.html: Less downward acceleration means a flatter trajectory.
